title: Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless v. Barry (1997)
shortTitle: Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless v. Barry (1997)
summary: The court looked for mandatory limits on shelter-allocation discretion and found no protected entitlement; its rejection of a statutory disclaimer was arguably dicta.

sections.Parties: The Washington Legal Clinic for the Homeless and other plaintiffs challenged District of Columbia documentation requirements for emergency shelter eligibility.
sections.Material Facts: The city’s code stated that it created no entitlement to shelter. The plaintiffs nonetheless alleged that the documentation policies violated procedural due process. Available shelter space was limited, and the relevant laws did not confine allocation discretion with mandatory criteria.
sections.Procedural History: The D.C. Circuit found no protected property interest under the applicable legal standards.
sections.Issue: Did the disclaimer itself settle whether shelter applicants held a protected property interest, and did the substantive law create such an interest under Roth?
sections.Holding: The court rejected reliance on the disclaimer as dispositive but found no discretion-constraining language sufficient to create the claimed entitlement.
sections.Reasoning: Roth directed attention to operative legal constraints on official discretion. Because those constraints were absent, the court could reject the due-process claim without giving independent force to the disclaimer. The editors accordingly caution that its treatment of the disclaimer may be dicta.

topics.lrs-o-new-property: The absence of mandatory allocation limits defeated the claimed shelter entitlement regardless of skepticism about the disclaimer.
topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: Barry applies the protected-interest threshold of the procedural due process framework to shelter allocation.
